title: Comfrey
subtitle: The external wound herb: salves, compresses, and poultices for bruises, strains, and skin repair
excerpt: Comfrey is a deep-rooted hedgerow plant whose leaf and root have a centuries-long use as an external wound and tissue-repair herb. The dried leaf is prepared as a compress for bruises and sprains; the root, extracted into oil and made into a salve, is applied to minor skin damage and muscle strains. Comfrey is strictly for external use only, never taken internally. A jar of dried leaf keeps 12 months.
sourceNotes: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), comfrey entry, Botanical.com transcription. glossaryTerms.definition: A herb or preparation traditionally applied externally to support the healing of minor wounds, bruises, and skin damage.
Compounds found in comfrey root (and to a lesser degree the leaf) that are hepatotoxic if taken by mouth over time. This is why comfrey is restricted to external use only.

content.text: Symphytum officinale L., family Boraginaceae. A robust perennial, 50 to 120 cm, with large, rough, lanceolate leaves covered in stiff hairs that can cause mild skin irritation. Flowers are bell-shaped, white to purple, drooping in clusters. Found in damp meadows, riverbanks, and waste ground across Europe. widely naturalised. The deep, fleshy taproot is large and black outside, white and gel-rich inside, it was historically known as "knitbone" for its traditional use on fractures and sprains. Both leaf and root are used externally. the root has the higher pyrrolizidine alkaloid content.
The leaf and root carry allantoin (a wound-healing compound), rosmarinic acid, and the
. Allantoin supports the soothing and tissue-repair action on intact skin. The alkaloids are the reason comfrey is restricted to external use.

The 20th-century herbalist Grieve records comfrey's use for bruises, sprains, fractures, and as a poultice for inflamed joints. The 17th-century herbalist Culpeper recommended it for "broken bones and dislocations." The traditional use was, until the 1980s, both internal and external. Internal use is now no longer appropriate, following research showing long-term oral use of PAs can harm the liver. The same alkaloid exposure. The current European herbal guidance reference entry (2011, revised) restricts use to external preparations, with the maximum exposure limits above.

Leaf compress: 2 tablespoons of dried comfrey leaf per 200 ml of just-boiled water, steeped 10 minutes, cooled to a comfortable temperature, strained. Soak a clean cloth and apply to intact unbroken skin over a bruise or sprain for 20 to 30 minutes. Up to twice a day, for a maximum of 10 days per course.

Root-infused oil and salve: 1 part dried comfrey root to 5 parts olive oil, double boiler at 60 to 65°C for 3 to 4 hours, strained. For a salve: melt 1 part beeswax to 4 parts infused oil, pour into tins at around 60°C. Apply to intact skin over bruises, strains, and minor muscle aches. 10-day course limit per the European herbal guidance guidance.

Course limits: current herbal guidance sets a maximum of 10 days per course and 4 to 6 weeks per year for external comfrey preparations. This is due to absorption of PAs through the skin with extended use.
Open wounds: never apply comfrey to open wounds, broken skin, or puncture wounds. The allantoin promotes surface skin closure which can trap infection in deeper tissue.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding: avoid all external comfrey preparations. PAs can cross the skin and may affect the unborn or nursing baby.
